title: Capt. Will & the hunting ground
summary: Kentucky's hunting grounds were not empty, and Shawnee and Cherokee hunters saw Virginia long hunters like Daniel Boone as poachers of their game.
bodyMarkdown:
Captain Will Emery, as tradition names him, led the hunters who found Daniel Boone in Kentucky's hunting grounds, which were not empty. The [Shawnee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shawnee) hunted across the larger northern and central parts of the country, and the Cherokee hunted closer to Cumberland Gap. To both nations, Virginia [long hunters](https://grokipedia.com/page/Longhunter) who stayed for months and stacked pelts for eastern markets were poachers taking the game their families depended on.

Daniel Boone was one of them. In 1769 he and John Stewart, with others guided by [John Finley](/stories/john-finley-the-trader-who-put-kentucky-on-boones-map/), came through Cumberland Gap and spent months hunting and gathering skins (see [Pilot Knob, Boone's Overlook](/stories/pilot-knob-boones-overlook-1769/)). On December 22, 1769, near the [Kentucky River](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kentucky_River), a party of Native hunters captured Boone and Stewart.

Boone's own account, told to John Filson and published in 1784 in [The Discovery, Settlement and Present State of Kentucke](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/909), is brief. The captors plundered them and held them for seven days, and the two men escaped at night and found their camp plundered and their companions gone. Filson's text names no captor.

Later writers told a fuller story. Archibald Henderson's [Conquest of the Old Southwest](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2390) (1920), chapter X, describes a Shawnee party returning from a hunt on the Green River and led by "Captain Will." In this version the Shawnee took the skins and horses and told them to go home and stay away, warning that the "wasps and yellow jackets" would sting if they returned.

John Bakeless, in [Daniel Boone](https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015%2E58770) (1939), adds that the two were released with moccasins and a trade gun, tried to recover their horses, and were captured again before escaping.

The warning-and-release story comes from later family tradition and does not appear in Boone's 1784 account. The name "Captain Will" (sometimes Will Emery) also comes from tradition. A 1774 letter in the Draper Manuscripts, cited secondhand, describes him as a man of mixed descent and Cherokee ties who lived and hunted with the Shawnee.

Native parties treated long hunters as poachers, according to the [Kentucky Historical Society](https://history.ky.gov/stories-and-blogs/kentuckys-long-hunters-pelts-profits-and-the-push-for-westward-expansion), and taking the skins was a way to defend a hunting ground. Bakeless records that Boone met Captain Will again in 1778, when Shawnee warriors captured him at the Blue Licks salt springs.

## Kentucky today

The [Shawnee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shawnee) today are three federally recognized tribes in Oklahoma: the [Absentee-Shawnee Tribe of Indians](https://grokipedia.com/page/Absentee_Shawnee_Tribe_of_Indians), the [Eastern Shawnee Tribe](https://grokipedia.com/page/Eastern_Shawnee_Tribe_of_Oklahoma) and the [Shawnee Tribe](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shawnee_Tribe). They carry the history of the people who once hunted these grounds, and the land Boone crossed is better understood as a contested commons than as an empty wilderness.
